notesStmt.note: Whitman probably wrote this manuscript in June 1887. In a letter to William Sloan Kennedy dated July 13, 1887, he sent a "slip copy" of this poem (presumably one of the copies printed for him by the jobber printer Henry Curtz, to whom the note on the reverse is addressed). He explained that he had written it for a "New York newspaper syndicate (S. S. McClure, Tribune Building)," which paid him $25 (See Reminiscences of Walt Whitman [London: Alexander Gardner, 1896], 55). Its reprinting in the 9 July 1887 issue of the Pall Mall Gazette was accompanied by a note explaining that Whitman had sent to them "an advance proof of [the poem] which was to be published in America . . . on the Fourth of July."

note.p: "The Dying Veteran" was first published in several newspapers nearly simultaneously between 2 and 4 July 1887. It was later reprinted in November Boughs (1888).

lg.head: The Dying Veteran
lg.note: [A Long Island incident, early part of the present century.]
lg.l: Amid the days of order, ease, ease, prosperity,
Amid the ‸current songs of beauty, peace, decorum,
I cast a reminiscence—(likely 'twill offend you,

I knew heard it in my boyhood)—More than a gen⹀
erationgeneration
since,

From Revolutionary times A queer a A queer old savage man,
a fighter under Washington himself,

Large, brave, cleanly, hot⹀blooded, no talker, rather
spiritualistic,

(‸Had Fought in the ranks—fought well—had been all
through the ‸rRevolutionary war,)

Lay dying—sons, daughters, church⹀deacons lovingly
tending him

Sharping their sense, their ears, toward his
‸murmuring,rambling, half⹀caught words:
"Let me return again to my war⹀days,
Body and soul to my war⹀days,
To ‸the sights and scenes—‸—to forming the line of battle,
To the cannons, the grim artillery,
To the galloping aids, carrying orders,
The wounded, the fallen, the heat, the suspense,
The perfume strong, the smoke, the deafening noise;
Away with your life of peace!—your joys of peace!
Give me the my old wild battle⹀joys life again!"
